Perfect numbers. A perfect number is a positive integer equal to the sum of its proper divisors—all divisors except the number itself. The first perfect number is six, which equals one plus two plus three. Perfect numbers are exceedingly rare. Only fifty-one are known, and the largest has over forty-one million digits. They carry deep historical and mystical significance, studied since antiquity, and are intimately connected to Mersenne primes through the Euclid-Euler theorem.

Here's the definition. A perfect number n satisfies sigma of n minus n equals n, where sigma of n is the sum of all divisors including n itself. Equivalently, the sum of the proper divisors equals n. The first four perfect numbers are six, twenty-eight, four hundred ninety-six, and eight thousand one hundred twenty-eight. Each was discovered centuries apart, showing how rare they truly are. A profound open problem remains: whether odd perfect numbers exist. If one does exist, it must exceed ten to the fifteen hundredth power. The Euclid-Euler theorem provides the complete characterization: an even number is perfect if and only if it has the form two to the power p minus one times the quantity two to the power p minus one, where two to the power p minus one is a Mersenne prime. Because of this theorem, finding perfect numbers reduces entirely to finding Mersenne primes. Computationally, this is done using the Lucas-Lehmer test, an efficient algorithm for testing Mersenne primes. The fifty-first known perfect number, discovered in twenty eighteen, has forty-nine million seven hundred twenty-four thousand ninety-five digits. To put that in perspective, writing it out would fill roughly a million pages. The concept generalizes through aliquot sums: a number's aliquot sum is the sum of its proper divisors. Perfect numbers are the special case where the aliquot sum equals the number itself.
